title: Landsmen abroad: keeping Drohiczyn connected through aid
summary: The records show emigrants building organizations and sending substantial assistance back to their hometown, extending community ties across the Atlantic.

editorialConnections.recordTitle: Founding of the Chicago Drohiczyn Support Association

editorialContent:
![Drohiczyn, the town whose Jewish community remained connected to its emigrants](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/7d/Flag_of_Drahi%C4%8Dyn.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=api&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)

## A bond made practical

For Drohiczyn’s emigrants, the hometown bond was more than nostalgia. It could mean money for food, heat, medical care, or the rebuilding of communal institutions. The memorial book remembers that connection through committees, societies, named donors, and funds sent across the Atlantic. Its accounts show that aid was not one continuous organization: groups formed, paused, changed names, and responded to different crises.

The book says the first Chicago [Drohiczyn Aid Association](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_e00a81f5db334c9834668989) began as an Aid Committee at the start of the First World War. After the Polish-Russian war, it recalls, help began arriving from America, including money carried to Drohiczyn by [Eliyahu Eisenstein](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_ef8e99d07359fec0d9a956b2), a delegate. The account presents a personal channel alongside organized fundraising: relief depended both on committees abroad and on people able to travel, learn what was needed, and deliver assistance.

The wider record places Drohiczyn in a region repeatedly caught between political powers. The town—also called Drahichyn or Drogichin—was within interwar Poland before Soviet and German occupation during the Second World War. The memorial book’s story of aid therefore spans not only migration but upheaval that could disrupt livelihoods and communications. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drahichyn?utm_source=openai))

## Chicago’s committee and the 1917 account

An old minutes book, quoted in the memorial book, provides a strikingly exact figure: the [Chicago Relief Committee](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_801f5e402b6b74fe3aa174c4) sent $2,152.72 to Drohiczyn. The same passage names [Tsvi Hakman](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_20f2c8012073f76a36549d9c) as chair, Zalman Eisenstein as treasurer, and Leibl Barenboim as secretary. It also lists Yisrael Baruch Eisenstein, Lane Goldberg, and Israel-Baruch Warschawski. A connected record identifies [Zalman Eisenstein](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_9b756c38153b0702b97a25a5) as treasurer and [Leibl Barenboim](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_4bd220616f9e9a0d17b81465) as secretary; these names make visible the work behind a remittance.

The minutes also credit a separate [Club Association](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_4d1331e3d36afd7f652e0c6b) with a $300 contribution. Its committee included [Tsipah Shevinski](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_072e3507722c0bd2c88b8670), [Moses Gratch](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_2363cc85547e62b6a0e2f6ab), and [Lane-Reizl Goldberg](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_31a8e8f1e9ac499c90bcece0). The book preserves the sum and roster, but does not specify the precise distribution of the 1917 funds. It would be misleading to assign them to particular households or projects without further evidence.

The memorial volume separately describes [Yisrael Baruch Eisenstein](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_31bd35344c4f058a137d7ff6) as a leading supporter of the hometown and says he helped organize relief in Chicago. It recounts that Eliyahu traveled to Drohiczyn and distributed funds. These passages illuminate the human links behind the committee’s work, but are not independent confirmation of the minutes’ dollar figure.

## From emergency relief to continuing support

According to the book, the early Chicago committee sent thousands of dollars after the war. Its account says American funds helped rebuild houses of study, the Talmud Torah, a public bath and mikveh; they also fed people in need and assisted merchants and workers who had lost income. In the mid-1920s, the book says, improving circumstances reduced the need for regular American relief, and the committee was disbanded. These claims are the community’s retrospective account; the translated page does not provide separate accounting records for each project.

Need returned in a different form. The book describes a large meeting in 1933 at Chicago’s Kehilat Yaakov synagogue, which established the [Chicago Drohiczyn Support Association](/communities/drohiczyn/records/event_candidate_6bd3815ab2cbdf64d8595f52), with David Eisenstein as president. The organization later used the name Aid Society. The account says it sent money for Passover and the High Holidays, and supported the hospital, schools, health assistance, a hospice program, orphans, poor brides, and winter fuel. Its picture is of aid woven into ordinary communal life—not only emergency relief, but seasonal support and care for institutions.

The record also points beyond Chicago. In New York, [Agudat Achim Anshei Drohichin](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_264b1f144a9e3a2f4b948adc) maintained premises at 158 Henry Street. The memorial book’s account of New York’s aid society says one document from Drohiczyn recorded 4,291 zlotys distributed among 204 families. The two cities’ organizations should not be collapsed into one: the book presents distinct associations and figures, each a different trace of a dispersed hometown community.

## Aid after migration—and the limits of the record

Relief ran in both directions. Landsmen abroad sent money and supplies to Drohiczyn; emigrant associations also helped newcomers settle in America. The memorial book describes Chicago immigrants gathering for Sabbath meetings and mutual support, and recounts the New York and Chicago communities as places where Yiddish, synagogue life, and shared hometown memory sustained a practical bond. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/drohichyn/dro388.html?utm_source=openai))

The outside record helps establish the gravity of the town’s later fate, but does not independently verify the association’s remittances. Yad Vashem’s encyclopedia entry describes the wartime destruction of Drohiczyn’s Jewish community; the town article on Wikipedia likewise identifies German occupation and a ghetto. These sources provide historical context, not corroboration for the book’s committee rosters, sums, or aid projects. ([wwv.yadvashem.org](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=258&utm_source=openai))

The memorial book says the Chicago association continued until Drohiczyn’s destruction. That closing point gives the story its weight: a fundraising body built around family and hometown ties persisted while the community it served was being destroyed. The evidence supplied here does not establish what happened to every contributor, recipient, or relative, nor does it trace each transfer. Further research could begin with [David Eisenstein](research:David Eisenstein and the Chicago Drohiczyn Support Association records), [158 Henry Street](research:Agudat Achim Anshei Drohichin records at 158 Henry Street), and surviving minutes or correspondence behind the 1917 remittance.
